title: Complexity of behavior saturates soon after the simplest rules

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Complexity of behavior saturates soon after the simplest rules

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: As rules become progressively more complicated, overall behavior grows more complex only until the threshold of universality is reached, and since that threshold is very low, behavior beyond the very simplest rules of any kind should quickly become as complex as it will ever be—consistent with the Chapter 3 survey.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: So what this means is that if one looks at a sequence of systems with progressively more complicated rules, one should expect that the overall behavior they produce will become more complex only until the threshold of universality is reached.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 11, “The Notion of Computation”; section “The Significance of Universality in Rule 110” (from p. 690), p. 690. Scope: cellular automata, Turing machines and other simple programs enumerated by rule complexity

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch11-16: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.50

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The finite survey component is reproducible from public rules and software. The universal statement and causal identification of a low universality threshold remain underdetermined.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For specified enumerated rule families and complexity metrics, compute long-run behavioral statistics as description length increases and locate proven universal members. Early plateaus across preregistered metrics would support saturation within those families.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Finite simulations cannot establish asymptotic behavior or universality.

Results from selected rule orderings need not generalize across system types.

Behavioral complexity has many inequivalent metrics.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.45
analysis feasibility: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.35
data existence: 0.7
discriminating power: 0.4

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Small rule spaces can be enumerated and scored with public software in weeks, which is enough to test the predicted plateau for elementary cellular automata and small Turing machines. As complex as it will ever be depends on the chosen score, and a plateau in one family does not cover every kind of simple program. The result is a family of proxy tests rather than a decision of the full prediction.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Order rules by a fixed complexity of the rule table and score each evolution by a fixed measure such as compressibility or persistence of interacting localized structures. The claim is supported if the measure plateaus once a low rule complexity is passed, and refuted if it keeps rising across that range.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Behavioral complexity has several standard measures, and they need not plateau together.

Enumeration is feasible only for small rule spaces; larger neighborhoods are a different sample.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

operationalizability: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.5
data existence: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.6
